Develop Food Products from Suitable Plant Ingredients and By-Products

Thematic Area: Circular Food Innovation & Ingredient Valorisation

How might we turn a safe, suitable plant-based ingredient or food-processing by-product into a desirable product with viable economics?

Background

An Indonesian healthy-food retailer operates prepared-food lines using broadly the same raw ingredients sold in its stores. The opportunity is to develop additional food products from suitable plant ingredients and food-processing by-products.

The objective is to select a traceable input stream and develop a desirable product with viable processing and sales economics. Consistent ingredient quality, availability and handling are central to the product concept.

Relevant partners offer ingredient processing, fermentation, food formulation and commercialisation support. The collaboration connects input specifications, product development and quality controls with a clear customer proposition.

Significance of Problem

The key challenges are:

  • Missed product opportunities: Suitable ingredients offer limited commercial value without an appealing formulation and a practical route to market.
  • Processing costs: Handling, treatment, testing and packaging costs determine the net value recovered from a new product.
  • Input consistency: Reliable ingredient volumes and quality are essential for repeatable production and commercial scale.

Existing Efforts

  • Available partner experience: A food-and-beverage developer explores uses for spent tea leaves and related collaborations. A university bio-processed okara technology has an identified commercial route for soybean by-product ingredients and drinks.
  • First application: Choose one traceable input stream that meets agreed acceptance criteria. Develop a limited product concept and assess taste, product stability, production yield, cost and customer interest.
  • Collaboration focus: Match the selected ingredient with relevant processing expertise and set specifications, handling arrangements, capacity and commercial terms. Compare full production economics with existing ingredient uses and measure the value created by the new product.

Potential Market Size

  • Global upcycled-food market: The global upcycled food products market was valued at US$41.71 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach US$79.51 billion by 2034, with 7.47% annual growth during 2026–2034. The market covers food products that create value from suitable food ingredients and by-products.

Eligibility / Qualification

  • Technology readiness: Minimum technology readiness level 3 (TRL3).
  • NUS linkage: NUS student or graduate founder, or incubation through an NUS programme such as BLOCK71.
  • Local and overseas startups: Open to Indonesian and overseas startups.
  • Commitment: Complete the selection process and travel to Indonesia if selected.
